title: The Impostor Syndrome Files
author: Kim Meninger
description: A podcast exploring impostor syndrome through honest conversations with professionals and experts, focusing on practical strategies for managing self-doubt and building confidence in careers and leadership.

episodes.title: The Right Time Is Now
episodes.summary: Kim talks career pivots and self-discovery with entrepreneur Niki Lazaridou, including how core values help you tell genuine misalignment apart from impostor syndrome.

episodes.title: What's the Cost of Not Pivoting?
episodes.summary: Eight-time career pivoter Juliana Pereira on navigating uncertainty with curiosity and self-trust, and how to recognize when a change is needed.

episodes.title: Hidden Metrics
episodes.summary: Executive coach Nora Bouchard on defining success beyond standard performance metrics, and how internal measures grounded in your values strengthen decision-making.

episodes.title: Being More Intentional About Your Career
episodes.summary: Dr. Cynthia Bentzen-Mercer on why high achievers drift without intentional planning, with her ACES framework for recognizing natural talents and expanding a current role before job hunting.

episodes.title: Communicating More Effectively Under Pressure
episodes.summary: Leadership communications coach Salvatore Manzi shares techniques for introverts and analytical thinkers to contribute earlier in meetings, organize their thoughts under pressure, simplify complex ideas, and use frameworks to stay clear when responding quickly.

episodes.title: Gardens vs. Gold Mines
episodes.summary: Josh Block on leading a family business through curiosity and humility, and how developing people instead of extracting value creates a thriving culture.

articles.question: How do you speak up in meetings when you need time to think?
articles.metaDescription: Kim Meninger and coach Salvatore Manzi on contributing earlier in meetings, organizing thoughts under pressure, and using simple frameworks.
articles.intro: You speak up in meetings when you need time to think by contributing earlier than feels comfortable, using a simple framework to organize your thoughts on the fly, and saying less than you know. That's the advice leadership communications coach Salvatore Manzi shares with host Kim Meninger on The Impostor Syndrome Files. The episode is aimed squarely at introverts and analytical thinkers, the people who have the best idea in the room and share it in the parking lot afterward.

sections.heading: The problem isn't your thinking, it's the timing
sections.body:
Kim opens the conversation with a pattern she sees constantly in her coaching work. Thoughtful people sit in a fast-moving meeting, process what's being said, form a genuinely good view, and by the time it's fully formed the conversation has moved on. Then they replay the meeting and conclude they're not cut out for this.

Salvatore's reframe is that the quality of thinking is rarely the issue. The issue is the gap between when the thought is ready and when the meeting needs it. Fast-paced environments reward people who talk while they think. Analytical people prefer to think and then talk.

Neither style is wrong, but if you wait for a complete, polished thought every time, you'll be silent in most meetings. The rest of the episode is about closing that gap without pretending to be someone you're not.

sections.heading: Contribute earlier, even if it's small
sections.body:
One of the most practical points in the episode is to get into the conversation early. The host explains that the longer you stay silent, the higher the bar tends to feel for what you eventually say. Speak in the first few minutes and a simple question or observation is plenty. Wait half an hour and you'll feel like your first comment has to be brilliant.

Early contributions don't have to be conclusions. Asking a clarifying question, restating what you're hearing, or flagging something you'd like to come back to all count. They put you in the room as a participant, and they make it easier to speak again later.

The host adds that this is also a direct antidote to impostor feelings. Waiting for the perfect moment feeds the story that you don't belong. Speaking early, even imperfectly, starts to disprove it.

sections.heading: Use a framework so you don't have to build the structure live
sections.body:
The hardest part of speaking under pressure is organizing your thoughts and saying them at the same time. Salvatore's answer is to stop building the structure in the moment. Use a framework you've decided on in advance, so all you're doing live is filling in the slots.

The episode makes the case for simple, repeatable structures for responding quickly, so that when someone puts you on the spot, you don't have to figure out what shape your answer should take. You already know. You just need the content.

This is especially useful for analytical thinkers who tend to see all the nuance at once. A framework forces a sequence, and a sequence is what listeners can follow.

sections.heading: Simplify before you speak, not after
sections.body:
The last major theme is simplifying complex ideas. People who think deeply often try to bring the whole picture into the room: the caveats, the edge cases, the three ways this could go wrong. Salvatore's coaching, which he's applied with leaders presenting at the United Nations and with founders raising funding rounds, pushes in the other direction. Lead with the simplest version.

That doesn't mean dumbing it down. It means picking the one thing the room needs to hear first and holding the rest in reserve for the questions that follow. If nobody asks, the nuance wasn't needed for the decision.

Kim and Salvatore both note that this feels risky to people with impostor feelings, because saying less can feel like hiding how much you know. In practice it reads as clarity, and clarity is what gets analytical people heard.

keyTakeaways: Analytical thinkers rarely lack good ideas; they lose the timing window in fast meetings.
Speak early with something small, like a question, so the bar for your first comment stays low.
Decide on a simple response framework in advance so you're only filling in content under pressure.
Lead with the simplest version of your idea and keep the nuance for follow-up questions.
Contributing imperfectly and early is one of the most direct ways to undercut impostor feelings.

faq.q: Is it okay to say "let me think about that" in a meeting?
faq.a: The episode's emphasis is on contributing earlier and using a framework so you can respond in the moment. Buying time occasionally is fine, but relying on it every time keeps you out of the conversation.

faq.q: How can introverts get heard in fast-paced meetings?
faq.a: Salvatore's advice is to get in early with a small contribution, use a repeatable structure for your answers, and simplify your point before you speak rather than bringing every caveat into the room.

faq.q: Does needing time to think mean I'm not leadership material?
faq.a: No. Kim frames this as a style difference, not a capability gap. The skills in the episode are about adapting your timing and structure, not changing how you think.

articles.sourceNote: Based on The Impostor Syndrome Files episode "Communicating More Effectively Under Pressure" with guest Salvatore Manzi, released August 4, 2026, hosted by Kim Meninger.
